title: Pages & Layouts
summary: Pages show route content, while layouts provide shared structure around pages.

subtopics.title: Page file
subtopics.explanation: A `page` file defines the content shown at its route. The route comes from the folder path containing the file. It is like a room placed at a named address. Keep the page focused on what belongs at that destination, and verify direct visits and refreshes work. For example, a product page can own its product data while a shop layout owns shared navigation.

subtopics.title: Layout file
subtopics.explanation: A `layout` file wraps pages in its route segment. It is useful for shared navigation, sidebars, or consistent page framing. It is like a hallway connecting rooms on one floor. Layouts can preserve shared UI during navigation, so state placed there may live longer than page state. For example, a nested account layout can keep account tabs stable across child routes.

subtopics.title: Nested layouts
subtopics.explanation: Nested layouts add shared structure for deeper route groups. A dashboard can have one outer site layout and a second layout for its own navigation. It is like a building with a common entrance and a separate office floor. Add nesting when it reflects real shared structure, not merely to create more files. For example, the root layout can load shared fonts and include the document language.

subtopics.title: Root layout
subtopics.explanation: The root layout must include the document’s `<html>` and `<body>` elements. It is the outer shell for the application. It is like the building foundation that every room depends on. Set global metadata and shared providers at the right level, and avoid placing page-only content in the root. For example, do not put account-specific page text into a layout shared by unrelated routes.

subtopics.title: Page content
subtopics.explanation: Keep route-specific text and behavior in the page component. Put genuinely shared interface pieces in an appropriate layout or component. It is like keeping room details in the room while shared signs stay in the hallway. This makes routes easier to maintain and avoids accidental duplication. For example, refresh a nested URL directly to verify the server can render that route.

foundations.overview: In the Next.js App Router, folders and special files define page routes. A `page` file provides route-specific content, while a `layout` file wraps pages that share structure. Think of pages as rooms and layouts as the building’s shared hallway. The root layout supplies the document shell. Keep shared navigation in layouts and page-specific content in page components.
foundations.whyItMatters: Separating page content from shared layouts prevents duplication and clarifies which UI persists during navigation. Correct boundaries also help teams reason about routing and state.
foundations.browserPerspective: On first load the browser receives fully-rendered HTML for the whole layout→page tree. On subsequent in-app navigations, Next swaps only the changed page segment's RSC payload into the existing layout, so the browser keeps the persisted layout DOM and its state intact.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A dashboard app uses a root layout for fonts/providers, a `(dashboard)` layout for the sidebar and top bar, and individual pages for Overview, Settings, and Billing — so switching tabs keeps the sidebar mounted and scroll position preserved.
foundations.businessImpact: Persistent layouts make multi-page apps feel like single-page apps, improving perceived speed and engagement, while the file-based structure lets teams onboard quickly because the URL map mirrors the folder tree.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Co-locating routing, UI, loading, and error states by folder reduces wiring and keeps related code together. Shared layouts eliminate duplicated chrome and centralize providers, cutting boilerplate across pages.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because layouts don't re-render on navigation, layout-level data fetches and expensive components aren't repeated per page. Pairing layouts with `loading.tsx` enables streaming and instant navigation feedback.
commonUseCases: Root layout for the html/body shell, fonts, and global providers
Section layouts for sidebars and nav bars that persist across pages
Templates for per-navigation animations or analytics that need a fresh mount
Per-page or per-section metadata for SEO and social previews

commonMisconceptions.myth: A folder is a route as soon as it exists.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A folder is only navigable once it contains a `page.tsx` (or a route handler). Without one, the folder is just structure and returns a 404.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Layouts re-render when you navigate between their child pages.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Layouts persist — they stay mounted and keep their state across navigations within their subtree. Use a `template.tsx` if you actually want a fresh instance per navigation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A layout is copied fresh into every page and cannot preserve UI.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Layouts can remain shared during navigation and may preserve state across child routes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Putting all page content in the root layout reduces duplication.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The root should provide shared shell; route-specific content belongs in page files.

visualExplorer.caption: Walk a request to /dashboard/settings through the nested layout tree down to the page.

config.intro: Follow how Next.js assembles the UI tree from the root layout down to the matching page.

steps.name: Root layout
steps.detail: app/layout.tsx renders <html>/<body>, global fonts and providers, and a {children} slot. It applies to every route and never unmounts.

steps.name: Section layout
steps.detail: app/dashboard/layout.tsx renders the sidebar/top bar and a {children} slot. It wraps everything under /dashboard and persists across dashboard pages.

steps.name: Page
steps.detail: app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx provides the unique content for /dashboard/settings, slotted into the nearest layout's {children}.

steps.name: Special files
steps.detail: loading.tsx and error.tsx for the segment wrap the page in Suspense/error boundaries without disturbing the surrounding layouts.

steps.name: Navigate
steps.detail: Going to /dashboard/billing swaps only the page segment; the root and dashboard layouts stay mounted with their state intact.

steps.name: Metadata merge
steps.detail: metadata from root, section layout, and page merge top-down to produce the final <head> for the route.

interactiveExamples.title: Layout persists, page swaps (runnable)
interactiveExamples.explanation: This simulates the App Router behavior: the surrounding layout (with a counter) stays mounted while the inner 'page' content changes — just like real layouts persist across navigation.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Increment the sidebar counter, then switch pages — the counter keeps its value because the layout stays mounted.

interactiveExamples.title: Root layout, metadata, and nesting (illustrative)
interactiveExamples.explanation: Server-side App Router file structure can't run in the browser, so this is illustrative: it prints the real files you'd create and how they nest. The real code is in the explanation/example fields.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Shows the nested files for a route and a sample root-layout metadata export.

codeLab.title: Build a persistent layout with a children slot
codeLab.instructions: Edit the Layout component so it renders a heading 'My App' and then renders its `children`. The App switches between two pages; confirm the heading stays put while the page content changes. Then Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A 'My App' header that stays visible while the page text switches between Home and About.
hints: A layout MUST render its `children` prop, or nested pages won't appear.
Put the shared header above {children}; everything inside {children} is the swappable page.

keyTakeaways: A `page` file defines the content shown at its route.
A `layout` file wraps pages in its route segment.
Nested layouts add shared structure for deeper route groups.
The root layout must include the document’s `<html>` and `<body>` elements.
Keep route-specific text and behavior in the page component.
